strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, Applied/Systems is more appropriate than Algorithms/General: the central contribution is an efficient, modular implementation. I therefore assess its integration, performance, and usability rather than requiring a new reconstruction algorithm.

Table 2 reports substantial end-to-end training improvements across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes on both A100 and RTX3090 GPUs, including improvements over the TamingGS-integrated baseline. Table 3 shows consistently higher PSNR and generally comparable or improved SSIM and LPIPS relative to original 3DGS.

The optimization choices have plausible profiling-based motivation. Figures 2–4 identify backward-rasterization and memory-access bottlenecks; Figure 5 supports improved cache locality, while Figures 6–7 demonstrate reductions in tile and fragment counts.

Decomposing the pipeline into accessible operators with Python and CUDA implementations could benefit Gaussian-splatting research. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges related techniques, including Morton ordering, DistWar, TamingGS, and gsplat.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the framework's advantage over its closest alternatives. There is no quantitative comparison with gsplat, despite modularity and usability being central claims, or with DistWar for reduction performance. Figure 1 suggests relative superiority without measurements. The TamingGS-integrated baseline also lacks quality results, preventing a complete speed–quality comparison.

Experimental control is unclear. Section 5 claims identical training parameters, but Section 4.2 explicitly changes density-management frequency and update sizes. These changes can affect Gaussian counts, quality, and workload. The manuscript needs exact schedules, final Gaussian counts, and controlled comparisons separating implementation gains from changes in training behavior.

The headline claim of approximately 30% lower GPU memory usage has no supporting measurements or measurement protocol. Likewise, the assertion that fused optimization supplies most of sparse Adam's acceleration is not supported by a fused-versus-sparse optimizer ablation.

Component-level performance evidence is insufficient. Cache-hit rates and operation counts support the motivation but do not quantify end-to-end contributions or overheads. Timed ablations are needed for clustering/compaction, tighter bounds, tile size, gradient compaction, and reduction, including reordering and binning costs.

The reduction pseudocode leaves consequential correctness questions unresolved. Algorithm 2 does not show initialization or per-Gaussian reset of validPixNum, and Algorithm 1 reduces tilesize² entries rather than the compacted valid count without specifying zero-filling. As written, this permits stale or uninitialized values to enter the sum. The t×α threshold also needs justification relative to the claimed preservation of 3DGS behavior. These may be documentation omissions, but no gradient checks or reference-equivalence tests resolve them.

Reproducibility and usability evidence are incomplete. The source-code availability statement has an empty link; training iteration counts, exact software versions, timing boundaries, and the reported COLMAP processing adjustments are unspecified. There are no concrete API examples, demonstrated extensions, or separate Python/CUDA performance measurements supporting the rapid-prototyping claim.

Presentation needs revision: Figure 1 has a placeholder caption, tighter-bound construction is not specified mathematically, and several implementation explanations are ambiguous. These editorial issues are secondary; the recommendation primarily reflects missing controlled evidence and unresolved technical details in an otherwise promising systems contribution.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, Applied/Systems better matches this framework paper. I assess it on implementation quality, practical utility, and demonstrated efficiency rather than requiring a new rendering algorithm. Faster, customizable Gaussian-splatting training is a relevant contribution to computer vision.

Table 2 reports substantial end-to-end training improvements across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes on both A100 and RTX3090 GPUs, including improvements over the TamingGS-integrated baseline. Table 3 shows consistently higher PSNR and comparable SSIM/LPIPS relative to the original 3DGS baseline.

The optimizations have a coherent systems motivation. Profiling identifies backward rasterization and memory-access bottlenecks; Figure 5 supports improved cache locality, and Figures 6–7 demonstrate reduced tile or fragment workloads. Decomposing the pipeline into accessible operators could also facilitate research extensions.
weaknesses: The experimental protocol does not establish a controlled comparison. Section 5 claims identical training parameters, but Section 4.2 explicitly changes density-control frequency and the scale of point additions/deletions. These changes can affect runtime, Gaussian counts, and reconstruction quality independently of kernel optimization. Exact schedules, training iteration counts, final Gaussian counts, and an experiment holding density control fixed are needed to interpret the speedups.

Comparison with the closest systems alternatives is insufficient. The paper identifies gsplat as an existing modular library but provides no measured comparison against it, despite Figure 1 suggesting a speed advantage. DISTWAR is discussed but not evaluated. The TamingGS-integrated baseline is useful, but its enabled features and configuration are unspecified, and its reconstruction quality is absent from Table 3. Consequently, the speed-quality advantage over the strongest evaluated baseline remains unclear.

The evidence does not isolate the contribution of the proposed components. Cache-hit rates and workload counts are helpful diagnostics, but there are no component-wise runtime ablations for clustering/compaction, tighter bounds, tile size, reduction, or optimizer changes. In particular, Section 4.4 attributes most of sparse Adam's acceleration to fusion without providing the dense/sparse and fused/unfused comparisons needed to support that claim.

Two central framework claims lack direct validation. The approximately 30% GPU-memory reduction asserted in the abstract and introduction has no accompanying memory measurements or measurement protocol. The usability claim has no concrete extension example, API demonstration, or comparison of Python/autograd and CUDA execution costs. These are substantive omissions for an Applied/Systems contribution.

The reduction description leaves correctness and compatibility unresolved. Algorithm 2 does not specify resetting validPixNum or initializing unused gradient entries, while Algorithm 1 sums over the full tile rather than the valid-fragment count. Algorithm 2 also filters gradients using transmittance times opacity greater than 1/255 without establishing equivalence to the baseline backward computation. These may be pseudocode omissions or deliberate approximations, but reference-gradient checks and explicit treatment of discarded contributions are needed to support the claim of preserving the core algorithm.

Reproducibility is limited: the source-code location in Section 4 is blank, the SfM/COLMAP adjustments acknowledged after Table 3 are unspecified, and essential implementation details such as the exact tighter-bound construction and claimed binning optimizations are missing. Software versions, evaluation splits/resolutions, and repeated-run variability are also not reported. Figure 1's placeholder caption and unsupported schematic ranking are smaller presentation issues; the main reason for weak rejection is that the promising efficiency results do not yet adequately substantiate the paper's comparative and framework-level claims.

strengths: LiteGS addresses a useful computer-vision systems problem: accelerating Gaussian-splatting training while preserving an accessible, modular implementation. Although no contribution type is declared, Applied/Systems is more appropriate than Algorithms/General; I therefore assess the integration and practical evidence without requiring a new reconstruction algorithm.

Table 2 reports consistent training-time improvements across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes on both A100 and RTX3090 GPUs, including improvements over the TamingGS-integrated baseline. These results suggest meaningful practical value.
Table 3 supports comparable reconstruction quality: LiteGS improves PSNR on every reported scene, matches or improves SSIM, and has mostly improved LPIPS with small regressions on three scenes.

The optimization choices are motivated by profiling. The cache-hit comparison, reduced tile counts for matched point clouds and camera poses, and fragment-count analysis provide useful evidence for the proposed memory-locality and workload-reduction mechanisms.

The separation into customizable pipeline stages with Python and CUDA interfaces is a promising design for research use. The manuscript appropriately attributes several underlying techniques, including Morton ordering and sparse optimization.
weaknesses: The experimental controls are insufficiently specified. Section 4.2 changes the frequency and scale of density-control operations, whereas Section 5 claims identical training parameters. Without the schedules, Gaussian counts, and a matched-schedule comparison, the reported speedups cannot be separated from changes to the optimization workload. Table 3 also omits quality results for the timed 3DGS-T baseline.

The most relevant modular-library baseline, gsplat, is discussed but not evaluated. Figure 1 positions LiteGS as faster without quantitative support. DistWAR is also cited without a direct reduction-kernel comparison. Consequently, the incremental systems contribution over closely related implementations remains unclear.

Several central claims lack direct evidence. The approximately 30% GPU-memory reduction has no supporting measurements or measurement protocol. The dual-interface usability claim has no extension example or Python-versus-CUDA performance comparison, limiting support for the framework's combined efficiency and usability contribution.

The diagnostic plots do not substitute for timing ablations. There is no component-wise assessment of clustering, compaction, tighter bounds, tile size, gradient compaction, and reduction, including their overheads. In particular, the claim that fusion accounts for most of sparse Adam's acceleration is not supported by a controlled fused-versus-sparse comparison.

Reproducibility is limited by missing training iteration counts, image resolutions, detailed configurations, software versions, and the unspecified COLMAP processing adjustments in Section 5.2. The source-code location in Section 4 is blank in the supplied manuscript. These omissions matter because runtime and quality depend strongly on the resulting scene representation and training configuration.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. Algorithm 2 does not show initialization or per-Gaussian resetting of the valid-fragment counter, while Algorithm 1 reduces over the full tile rather than the reported valid count; unused entries therefore need explicitly defined handling. The tighter bounding-box construction and the compatibility implications of the transmittance-weighted gradient cutoff also need clarification or numerical validation. These are unresolved specification concerns, rather than proof that the implementation is incorrect.

strengths: The strongest contribution is an Applied/Systems contribution, although no type is explicitly declared. I assess it accordingly: the integration of rasterization, spatial data organization, and densification is potentially valuable without requiring each component to be a fundamentally new algorithm.

Table 1 reports substantial practical improvements across three established datasets on a common RTX 3090. On Mip-NeRF 360, LiteGS-balance achieves 28.13 dB in 301 seconds with 1.10 million primitives, versus 28.08 dB in 3142 seconds with 3.21 million primitives for 3DGS-MCMC.

The one-warp-per-tile design has a clear computational motivation, and the scanline formulation and packed mixed-precision operations address the register-pressure tradeoff it introduces. Efficiently collecting densification statistics within this rasterizer provides a meaningful connection between system and algorithm design.

The experiments include useful component-level evidence. Table 2 shows substantial acceleration from clustering/culling with nearly unchanged quality, Table 3 compares rasterizer timings at three model sizes, and Table 4 supports the usefulness of the combined densification changes.
weaknesses: Important implementation details needed to reproduce the central results are missing: the densification threshold or selection rule, how the three model budgets are enforced, the accumulation/reset window for gradient statistics, and the precise construction and updating of cluster bounds. The manuscript claims an open-source release but provides no identifiable repository link.

The numerical reliability of the rasterizer is insufficiently established. FP16 transmittance and gradient accumulation and the integerized covariance-gradient reduction are described without comparisons against an FP32 reference, gradient-error measurements, or treatment of rounding and cancellation. Table 3 measures speed but does not establish equivalent rendering and backward-pass accuracy. Separate ablations of scanline evaluation and precision changes would clarify the source and cost of the gains.

Table 4 does not isolate opacity decay: its removal also restores the original densification hyperparameters and reset schedule. Consequently, the improvement cannot be attributed specifically to gentler opacity updates. The table also omits primitive counts and training times, leaving budget comparability unclear. Moreover, the proposed score is count-weighted variance, C_i Var, rather than variance alone; the effect of this visibility/footprint weighting is neither motivated nor ablated.

Systems evidence is narrower than the general claims. Rasterizer microbenchmarks cover only Garden on one GPU, with no register-occupancy, cache-miss, sorting-overhead, or peak-memory measurements. In particular, the claimed memory advantage and negligible statistics/reordering overhead are not quantified. A second GPU is not essential for acceptance, but the broad hardware claims require qualification.

Several claims exceed the reported evidence. All reported turbo dataset-average training times exceed one minute, so the title's 'Subminutes' claim is unsupported. Turbo also trades worse SSIM/LPIPS for speed relative to Mini-Splatting v2, and its 500k-primitive backward pass is slower than TC-GS. These remain useful tradeoffs, but do not support uniformly superior performance. No qualitative reconstructions or per-scene results are supplied to examine where quality is lost.

The mathematical specification needs correction: the stated 3D Morton interleaving uses 2k offsets instead of 3k and has inconsistent bit counts; Algorithm 1 uses an undefined d; and the rendering equations confuse covariance with inverse covariance and misindex transmittance. These could be presentation errors rather than implementation failures, but the missing code makes that distinction difficult. Together with the validation and reproducibility gaps above, they leave a slight preference for rejection despite promising aggregate results.

strengths: LiteGS addresses a practically important computer-vision bottleneck: efficient optimization of Gaussian scene representations. Its integration of warp-level rasterization, spatially coherent data management, and adaptive densification is a credible contribution even though several underlying techniques are established.

Table 1 reports substantial gains across three standard datasets on a common RTX 3090. On Mip-NeRF 360, LiteGS-balance achieves 28.13 dB in 301 seconds with 1.10M Gaussians, compared with 28.08 dB in 3142 seconds with 3.21M for 3DGS-MCMC. These results indicate a potentially valuable improvement in training efficiency and representation compactness.

The experiments examine multiple model budgets and include relevant accelerated and quality-oriented baselines. Table 2 supports the practical benefit of the clustering pipeline, while Table 3 provides operator-level timings rather than relying entirely on end-to-end comparisons affected by different densification trajectories.

The opacity-gradient disagreement intuition is plausible, and Table 4 consistently favors the complete densification strategy across datasets. The manuscript also acknowledges the lightweight model's LPIPS trade-off and the limitations of center-based spatial sorting.
weaknesses: The numerical correctness of the rasterizer is insufficiently validated. FP16 blending and gradient accumulation, together with exponent-aligned integer reduction for covariance gradients, change numerical behavior. The manuscript provides neither comparison against an FP32 reference on fixed inputs nor sufficient details about rounding, signed mantissas, and overflow handling. End-to-end reconstruction scores are encouraging but do not isolate errors introduced by these central optimizations.

The ablations do not establish several claimed mechanisms. Table 3 bundles warp assignment, scanline evaluation, mixed precision, and integer reduction without separating their effects. There are no register, occupancy, or cache measurements supporting the architectural explanations. Table 4 changes the reset policy and densification hyperparameters together, so its improvements cannot be attributed specifically to gentle opacity decay; it also omits Gaussian counts and timings for the variants.

The densification criterion needs stronger justification and specification. The implemented score is count-weighted variance, C_i Var, so it depends on pixel coverage and observation count as well as gradient disagreement. High variance can also arise from differing gradient magnitudes without conflicting directions. The paper does not examine these effects or explain the selection thresholds, statistic accumulation window, and budget-control procedure sufficiently for reproduction.

Several method descriptions contain consequential ambiguities or apparent errors. The Morton expression uses offsets 2k, 2k+1, and 2k+2 rather than the non-overlapping offsets required for three-coordinate bit interleaving, and its quantization width is inconsistent with the stated bit range. Algorithm 1 uses an undefined d for the quadratic coefficient. Equation 2 uses the declared covariance directly rather than its inverse, and Equation 1's transmittance recurrence appears shifted. These could be presentation errors, but the implementation must be clarified before correctness can be confidently assessed.

Experimental reporting limits independent verification. The supplied manuscript claims an open-source release but provides no repository link. Exact scene lists, evaluation splits, baseline configurations, timing boundaries, and run variability are not adequately documented. Table 4's full-model results also differ from Table 1 without identifying the configuration responsible. For a performance-centered contribution, these details matter.

Some headline claims exceed the evidence. The reported lightweight training times are 108–145 seconds, which do not demonstrate the title's subminute training. Table 3's 500k backward pass is slower than the Tensor-core baseline, and its combined forward/backward improvement there is only about 1.49× over that baseline. The claimed peak-memory advantage is not measured, and architectural generality is inferred from one GPU. Overall, the substantial reported gains make this a close decision, but unresolved correctness, attribution, and reproducibility concerns support a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The strongest contribution is an integrated training system. Although no contribution type is declared, Applied/Systems is more appropriate than Algorithms/General: the value lies in combining hardware-aware rasterization, spatial data organization, and densification to improve practical reconstruction efficiency.

Table 1 demonstrates substantial speed–quality improvements across three standard datasets. On Mip-NeRF 360, LiteGS-balance achieves 28.13 dB with 1.10 million primitives in 301 seconds, compared with 28.08 dB, 3.21 million primitives, and 3142 seconds for 3DGS-MCMC. These gains are practically meaningful even without requiring uniformly best reconstruction metrics.

The design has a coherent systems rationale. Assigning one warp per tile reduces gradient aggregation overhead, while scanline evaluation and mixed precision address register pressure. Efficient collection of per-pixel statistics also supports the proposed densification criterion, providing a concrete connection between system and algorithm design.

The experiments provide useful component-level evidence. Table 2 shows substantial training-time reductions from the clustering pipeline with little quality change; Table 3 compares rasterizers at three primitive counts; and Table 4 consistently favors the complete densification strategy across datasets. These results support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The ablations do not fully isolate the claimed mechanisms. Removing opacity decay also changes the densification hyperparameters and reset schedule, confounding attribution. Table 4 omits primitive counts and training times, so differences in model capacity or computation cannot be excluded. Table 3 evaluates the complete rasterizer without separately testing scanline evaluation, mixed precision, integer reduction, or tile size.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The manuscript claims an open-source release but supplies no repository link. It does not specify the variance threshold or budget-selection rule, the precise accumulation/reset window for gradient statistics, or complete split/prune settings. Scene lists, exact image resolutions, baseline configurations, and timing boundaries also need clearer documentation.

Numerical correctness of the rasterizer deserves direct validation. The integerized floating-point reduction lacks details about signed mantissas, overflow headroom, rounding, and cancellation. There is no comparison of forward outputs or gradients against an FP32 reference. Aggregate reconstruction scores are encouraging but cannot establish the accuracy of these individual approximations.

The densification interpretation is stronger than the evidence. The implemented score is count-weighted variance, C_i Var, which depends on projected footprint and observation frequency as well as gradient disagreement. High variance can also arise from unequal same-sign gradients. Comparisons with normalized variance and gradient magnitude under matched budgets would help establish that the benefit comes from detecting under-reconstruction.

Several claims exceed the reported evaluation. All Table 1 training times exceed one minute, so the title's 'subminutes' claim is unsupported by those results. LiteGS-turbo improves PSNR over Mini-Splatting v2 but has worse SSIM and LPIPS on all three datasets. Peak-memory advantages are asserted without measurements, and hardware generality is inferred from one RTX 3090. Speedy-Splat is discussed but not included in the empirical comparison.

There are correctable technical inconsistencies: Algorithm 1 uses an undefined d for the quadratic coefficient; the stated covariance is used where an inverse covariance is expected; the Morton-code quantization and bit-interleaving description are inconsistent; and Table 1 reports 0.780 SSIM in its caption where Table 2 reports 0.870 for the corresponding setting. These issues do not independently invalidate the empirical contribution, but they reduce confidence in implementation fidelity.
